common_name: Karenko Azalea (Two-Tone Sport of Juko Satsuki Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Karenko is a two-color sport of the influential Satsuki cultivar Juko and has itself become a widely used Satsuki breeding parent.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching to keep the shallow root system cool and evenly moist. Karenko arose as a two-color sport of Juko, trading its parent's solid medium pink for a bicolor flower pattern, and small dark green leaves and a mounding habit typical of its Juko lineage. It has in turn become an important breeding parent in its own right, standing behind named Satsuki hybrids such as Karenbana, Masazuki, and Aiko, and producing the white-based sport Byakuren. As with other Satsuki selections, flowering comes later in the season than most Kurume and Southern Indica azaleas, and the compact form suits border plantings, containers, and bonsai training alike. Water deeply during dry spells and prune only right after flowering, since this later-flowering type sets next year's buds soon after bloom ends.

common_name: Kiyoka Azalea (White-and-Purple Seedling of Kobai Satsuki Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Kiyoka is a seedling raised from the Satsuki cultivar Kobai and was registered in 2014, grown for its small flowers in white with purple secondary markings.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching to keep the shallow root system cool and evenly moist. Kiyoka was raised as a seedling of the older Satsuki cultivar Kobai and carries small, single flowers whose primary white ground is marked with purple secondary coloring, a departure from Kobai's own rose-red-and-white variegated blooms. It was formally registered in 2014 and remains a comparatively uncommon selection grown mostly among Satsuki collectors and bonsai enthusiasts rather than in general landscape trade. Like other Satsuki cultivars, it flowers later in the season than most Kurume and Southern Indica azaleas, typically in late spring to early summer, and its small leaves and modest stature suit container culture and bonsai training. Water deeply during dry spells and prune only right after flowering, since buds for the following year set soon after bloom ends.

common_name: Royalty Camellia (Large Deep Pink Japonica-Reticulata Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Royalty is a 1968 hybrid of Camellia japonica 'Clarise Carlton' and Camellia reticulata 'Chang's Temple', bred by T. Croson in California and introduced in 1970.

directions: Royalty combines Camellia japonica 'Clarise Carlton' with the reticulata cultivar Chang's Temple, pairing the reticulata parent's glossy, large-leafed vigor with somewhat better cold tolerance than a pure reticulata selection. Its very large, semi-double flowers open brilliant deep pink to red in early-to-mid season, set against shining, reticulata-type foliage on a slow-growing shrub that broadens with age. The cross earned an Award of Merit from camellia societies in 1986 and later a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit, reflecting its reliability as a garden plant beyond typical reticulata hardiness limits. Grow in humus-rich, acidic, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial shade sheltered from drying wind, watering regularly through the growing season and pruning lightly only right after bloom.
sources: American Camellia Society — ACS Camellia Encyclopedia
